abstract: Activity-dependent ubiquitination of synaptic proteins is one of the key contributors of synaptic plasticity, along with localized protein synthesis and ubiquitin-dependent protein turnover. Substantial changes in the protein composition occur in the postsynaptic density upon chronic activation or inhibition of primary neurons. Precisely how a large-scale regulation of ensembles of synaptic proteins occurs through the ubiquitin proteasome system remains unknown. MAGE-D1 is a highly conserved protein enriched in brain and its deletion in mice leads to a range of behavioral phenotypes including defects in learning, memory and a complete resistance to cocaine addiction. Here, we found that MAGE-D1 acts as a scaffold bridging the ubiquitin ligase Praja-1 and the deubiquitinase Usp7. This MAGE-D1 signalling module directly interacts with and regulates the levels of Brain acid-soluble protein-1 (BASP1) which is a key component and stabilizer of neuronal membrane rafts. Disruption of MAGE-D1 complex function or chemical inhibition of Usp7 in mice results in resistance to cocaine-induced locomotor sensitization accompanied by specific degradation of oligomeric BASP1 and other key synaptic proteins in the postsynaptic density of mice thalamus. As a result, loss of MAGE-D1 in differentiated neurons leads to a dramatic disorganization of neuronal membrane rafts and anomalies in the synaptic membrane protein landscape. Finally, we mapped the structural architecture of the human MAGE-D1/Praja-1/Usp7 complex revealing the basis for the scaffolding nature of MAGE-D1. In summary, we discovered a conserved synaptic ubiquitin signalling network mediated by a protein complex that localizes to the synapse and regulates structures of membrane rafts and actin cytoskeleton.
